name: Skin lightening pregnancy tablets

lead: Skin lightening pregnancy tablets are pills that, according to a 2020 Der Spiegel report summarised on Wikipedia, some pregnant women in Ghana take hoping their child will be born with fair skin.

The practice sits within wider skin-lightening culture in Ghana, where a preference for lighter skin has been documented since the 16th century. No published trial was found testing whether tablets alter a baby's skin colour.

paras: Reports describe women taking tablets during pregnancy, with some also applying bleaching lotion to babies. Specific products and amounts are not covered here.

Wikipedia notes pregnant users may face health complications for themselves and their children. Oral lightening agents such as glutathione have unclear effectiveness, and a baby's skin colour is determined by inheritance.

chain: Believed to influence the baby's pigmentation
angle.text: Users take the tablets with the aim of a lighter-skinned baby. The outcome is a belief held by users; no study of it was found.

lead: Skin lightening pregnancy tablets are pills that some pregnant women in Ghana reportedly take in the hope that their child will be born with fair skin, according to a 2020 Der Spiegel report cited by Wikipedia; some also apply bleaching lotion to babies.[1]

The practice is tied to a long-standing preference for lighter skin in Ghana, documented from the 16th century. Scholar Shirley Anne Tate links it to colonial-era aesthetics, and the Der Spiegel report quoted the view that light-skinned people earn more.[1] Wikipedia notes that pregnant users may face health complications, both for themselves and their children.[1]

paras: Oral agents used for skin whitening include glutathione, whose effectiveness is unclear, and tranexamic acid, with tentative support for melasma in one 2017 review and insufficient evidence in another.[1] Topical agents have documented risks, including mercury toxicity and hydroquinone-related ochronosis.[1]

timeline.event: Der Spiegel report describes pregnant women taking tablets hoping for fair-skinned children.[1]
